title: DOM & Rendering Pipeline
tagline: How the browser turns HTML and CSS into pixels: DOM, CSSOM, render tree, layout, paint, compositing, and the true cost of reflow.

sections.content:
Every time a browser loads a web page it performs a remarkable sequence of transformations. Raw bytes arrive over a network cable, get decoded into characters, parsed into a tree of objects, styled with cascading rules, measured and positioned on a two-dimensional canvas, painted into pixel buffers, and finally assembled and handed to the GPU to display on screen — all within a handful of milliseconds. This entire sequence is the **rendering pipeline**, and every front-end engineer should understand it deeply.

Why does this matter practically? Because the rendering pipeline determines the performance cost of everything you do in JavaScript. Reading `element.offsetWidth` after writing to the DOM can silently trigger an entire layout recalculation. Animating `width` instead of `transform` forces the browser to re-run the three most expensive stages sixty times per second. Adding an innocent `box-shadow` to a frequently-repainted element can cut your frame rate in half. The pipeline is the reason these things happen.

The browser is also remarkably clever about doing as little work as possible. It tracks which DOM nodes are dirty, limits repaints to changed regions, offloads certain animations to the GPU compositor thread so they never block JavaScript, and uses heuristics to promote frequently-moving elements to their own compositing layers. Understanding both the pipeline and these optimisations gives you a precise mental model for writing high-performance code.

This chapter builds that model from the ground up. We start with raw bytes and finish with pixels on screen, examining each stage in depth: what triggers it, what it costs, what the browser does to skip it when possible, and what programming patterns exploit or accidentally destroy those optimisations.

sections.title: Rendering as a Newspaper Printing Press
sections.content:
Imagine the browser as a sophisticated newspaper printing press with six distinct stations:

**Station 1 — DOM (the article archive)**: Reporters file every article, headline, photo, and caption. These are pure content — no decisions about layout have been made yet. Editors can add, remove, or rewrite articles at any time.

**Station 2 — CSSOM (the style guide)**: A separate team maintains the house style guide: typefaces, column widths, colours, margins. Every possible combination of element types and classes has a computed style rule.

**Station 3 — Render Tree (the page blueprint)**: The layout team cross-references articles with the style guide and produces a blueprint of only the visible content — classified ads marked 'do not print' (`display: none`) are excluded entirely. Every visible item gets its final resolved styling attached.

**Station 4 — Layout (the typesetter)**: A skilled typesetter physically measures every column, wraps every line of text, positions every photo box, and records the exact coordinates of every element on the page. This is slow, painstaking work.

**Station 5 — Paint (the printer)**: The printing press applies ink to paper, rasterising text, borders, backgrounds, and shadows into actual pixels. Complex graphics (gradients, drop shadows) take longer to render.

**Station 6 — Composite (stacking the sheets)**: The finished press sheets are stacked in the right order. Some sections (adverts, inserts) are printed separately and overlaid at the end — these are **compositor layers**.

If a reporter changes an article mid-print (`DOM mutation`), the press must re-run the typesetter (`reflow`) and re-ink the changed sections (`repaint`). But if only the opacity of an overlay advert changes, the press can simply adjust the stacking without touching any other station — the compositor handles it in isolation, which is orders of magnitude cheaper.

sections.title: Stage 1: Building the DOM
sections.content:
When the browser receives an HTML response, it processes it through a **byte stream decoder** (interpreting character encoding such as UTF-8), then a **tokeniser** that recognises tags and attributes, and finally a **tree constructor** that builds the DOM.

The **Document Object Model** is a tree of node objects. Every element is an `Element` node, text content is a `Text` node, comments are `Comment` nodes, and at the root sits the `Document` node. HTML5 parsers are deliberately fault-tolerant — the spec defines exact error recovery rules so that malformed markup produces a predictable DOM rather than an error page.

Critically, **the DOM is not the HTML**. The DOM is a live in-memory object graph. JavaScript can mutate it at any time: appending children, changing attributes, removing nodes. When you call `document.createElement('div')` or set `innerHTML`, you are directly modifying this object graph.

The DOM also does not include display information. It is purely structural. A node in the DOM has no concept of 'where it appears on screen' — that computation happens later. This is an important architectural separation.

**Parser-blocking scripts** complicate DOM construction. When the HTML parser encounters a `<script>` tag without `async` or `defer`, it stops building the DOM, downloads the script, executes it (because the script might call `document.write` to modify the stream), and only then resumes parsing. This is why scripts at the bottom of `<body>` or with `defer` load faster — they do not block parsing.

Modern browsers also run a **speculative preload scanner** that looks ahead in the HTML stream in parallel with the parser, discovering resources like images, stylesheets, and scripts early so they can begin downloading before the main parser reaches them.

sections.title: Stage 2: Building the CSSOM
sections.content:
CSS bytes are processed through an identical pipeline: bytes → characters → tokens → parse tree → CSSOM. The **CSS Object Model** is a tree that mirrors the DOM structure and stores resolved style information for every possible node.

CSS parsing has one critical property that HTML parsing does not: it is **render-blocking**. The browser will not render a single pixel until all CSS in `<link>` and `<style>` tags has been downloaded and parsed. Why? Because a stylesheet loaded later could completely change the visual appearance of elements already parsed. Rendering partial CSS would produce a **flash of unstyled content (FOUC)** — a brief moment where the page appears without styling. Browsers avoid this by blocking rendering until the CSSOM is complete.

This means that large, slow-loading CSS files directly delay First Paint. The fix is not to avoid CSS, but to keep critical CSS small, inline it in `<style>` tags in the document head, and use `media` attributes on `<link>` tags to mark non-critical CSS as non-blocking (the browser still downloads it, just without blocking rendering).

Style resolution in the CSSOM involves **cascade** (which rule wins when multiple rules match the same element), **specificity** (ID selectors beat class selectors beat tag selectors), and **inheritance** (many properties like `color` and `font-size` propagate from parent to children). The output for each element is a set of **computed values** — percentages resolved to pixels, `em` values resolved to absolute pixel sizes, `inherit` replaced by the actual inherited value, `initial` replaced by the property's default.

An important subtlety: **JavaScript and CSSOM**. Accessing `getComputedStyle()` from JS reads CSSOM values. But if a JS `<script>` appears after a `<link rel=stylesheet>`, the browser must also wait for the CSSOM before executing the script — because the script might call `getComputedStyle`. So script execution is also style-blocked, which is another reason `defer`/`async` matter.

sections.title: Stage 3: The Render Tree — Merging DOM and CSSOM
sections.content:
The **Render Tree** is built by walking the DOM tree and attaching computed CSSOM information to each visible node. It is neither the DOM nor the CSSOM — it is a new, third tree that represents exactly what needs to be drawn on screen.

The most important rule: **display:none elements are excluded from the Render Tree**. They exist in the DOM, they consume JavaScript query results, but they have no presence in the Render Tree and contribute zero cost to layout and paint. This is fundamentally different from `visibility: hidden` — a hidden-but-visible element **is** in the Render Tree; it occupies space, it participates in layout, it just renders as transparent.

Some things appear in the Render Tree but not the DOM: **CSS pseudo-elements** (`::before`, `::after`, `::first-line`). These are generated by CSS rules and inserted into the Render Tree as if they were child nodes, even though no corresponding DOM node exists. You can style them and they affect layout, but you cannot select them with `querySelector`.

The Render Tree also reflects the **stacking context** model — which elements stack on top of which others, determined by `z-index`, `position`, `opacity`, `filter`, `transform`, and `will-change`. Stacking contexts are subtrees of the Render Tree that are painted as a unit. A child with `z-index: 999` cannot escape its stacking context parent's paint order — a common source of `z-index` confusion.

Building the Render Tree is relatively cheap. The expensive steps come next.

sections.title: Stage 4: Layout (Reflow) — Computing Geometry
sections.content:
**Layout** (also called **reflow**) is the process of computing the exact position (x, y) and size (width, height) of every Render Tree node in the viewport's coordinate system. This is the most expensive stage in the pipeline for large, complex documents.

Layout uses the **CSS box model**: every element is a rectangular box with content, padding, border, and margin regions. Layout must account for block formatting contexts, inline formatting contexts (text line-wrapping), flexbox algorithms, grid placement algorithms, float clearing, and absolute/fixed/sticky positioning.

The fundamental difficulty is **interdependence**. The size of a parent often depends on the sizes of its children (e.g., a `div` with `height: auto`). A child's size may depend on its percentage-based width relative to its parent. Flexbox children negotiate sizes with siblings. This means layout sometimes requires **multiple passes** through the tree — a phenomenon called **layout thrashing** at the algorithmic level, distinct from the JavaScript thrashing discussed below.

**What triggers a full or partial reflow?**
- Adding or removing a DOM node
- Changing the text content of a node
- Changing any geometry-affecting CSS property: `width`, `height`, `padding`, `margin`, `border`, `font-size`, `font-family`, `line-height`, `display`, `position`, `flex-*`, `grid-*`
- Resizing the viewport (triggers a global reflow)
- Reading certain layout properties from JavaScript (forced synchronous layout)

Browsers optimise by maintaining a **dirty region** — marking only the subtrees that need to be re-laid-out. A change deep in an isolated absolutely-positioned subtree may not require recomputing the entire document. But changes to an element in normal document flow can cascade widely.

**Forced Synchronous Layout (FSL)** is a particularly important concept. The browser batches DOM mutations and defers layout until the next frame. But if JavaScript reads a layout-dependent property (`offsetWidth`, `getBoundingClientRect`, `scrollTop`, `getComputedStyle`) while there are pending mutations, the browser **must** flush and compute layout immediately — synchronously — before returning the value. This is called a forced synchronous layout. It is not a bug in the browser; it is a necessary guarantee that your read returns a fresh value. The problem arises when you read and write alternately in a loop: every read after a write forces a new layout, creating N layout passes instead of one.

sections.title: Stage 5: Paint (Rasterisation) — Converting Geometry to Pixels
sections.content:
**Paint** (also called **rasterisation**) converts the abstract layout boxes from the previous stage into actual pixel colors stored in memory buffers. Each element's paint record describes how to draw it: fill rectangles, stroke borders, render text glyphs, apply box shadows, draw background images.

The browser does not paint the entire page into a single bitmap. It divides the page into **tiles** — typically 256×256 or 512×512 pixel regions — and paints each tile independently. This allows the browser to prioritise painting tiles near the viewport and to skip tiles that are far off-screen. Tiles are rendered by **raster threads** (often multiple, running in parallel) and their pixel data is uploaded to the GPU as textures.

**What triggers a repaint (without reflow)?**
Changing any CSS property that affects appearance but not geometry:
- `color`, `background-color`, `border-color`
- `box-shadow`, `text-shadow`
- `outline`
- `visibility` (not `display` — changing display triggers reflow)
- `background-image`

Paint cost is proportional to the **painted area** and the **complexity of the effects** being rendered. A large element with a complex multi-layer gradient and drop shadow is expensive to paint. This is why `box-shadow` is cited as a paint performance concern — it is computationally expensive to rasterise.

Browsers maintain a **paint invalidation region** — only tiles containing changed pixels are repainted. If a small spinner in the corner of the screen rotates, only the tiles covering that spinner need repainting (unless the spinner is animating via a layout-triggering property, in which case the cost is much higher).

**Paint and stacking order**: elements are painted in **stacking order**, not DOM order. Background, borders, floated elements, inline elements, and positioned elements are painted in a specified sequence per the CSS Painting Order spec. Getting the stacking order wrong in your mental model can cause confusion about why `z-index` does not work as expected.

sections.title: Stage 6: Composite — GPU Assembly
sections.content:
**Compositing** is the final stage: painted layer textures are sent to the GPU, which assembles them in the correct order and writes the final frame to the display's frame buffer. This stage runs on the **compositor thread** — a separate thread from the main JavaScript thread — which is why compositor-only operations can be smooth even when the main thread is busy.

The key insight: if an animation only changes **composited properties** (`transform` and `opacity`), the browser can re-composite existing layer textures at each frame without re-running layout or paint at all. The GPU applies a matrix transform to an already-painted texture — an operation that takes microseconds rather than milliseconds. This is the fundamental reason `transform`-based animations are smooth and `width`-based animations are not.

**Compositor layers** are promoted when the browser determines that an element will move or change frequently. Promotion criteria include:
- `will-change: transform` or `will-change: opacity`
- `transform: translateZ(0)` or `transform: translate3d(0,0,0)` (the old hardware-acceleration hack)
- `position: fixed` or `position: sticky`
- `<video>`, `<canvas>`, `<iframe>` elements
- Elements with CSS animations or transitions involving `transform` or `opacity`

Each promoted layer is an independent GPU texture. During compositing, the GPU blends these textures together with any required transforms applied. The compositor thread maintains the layer tree and handles scrolling — which is why most scrolling on modern browsers is smooth even on pages with heavy JavaScript: scroll position is updated on the compositor thread without involving JS at all.

**The GPU memory trade-off**: each compositor layer consumes GPU texture memory. A 1000×1000 pixel element at 32bpp uses ~4MB of GPU memory. Promoting too many elements runs out of GPU memory, forcing layers to be evicted and re-uploaded — which can actually cause jank. The rule: only promote elements that genuinely need it, and remove `will-change` after the animation ends with `el.style.willChange = 'auto'`.

**`filter` and `backdrop-filter`** added to an element that already has a compositor layer also run on the GPU. But if the element is not already on its own layer, a complex filter forces promotion — and affects all siblings in the stacking context, potentially promoting them too. This is a subtle cause of unexpected memory spikes.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The bad pattern forces N synchronous layout calculations — one per element — because every read follows a write. The good pattern batches reads before writes, allowing the browser to perform only one layout at frame time. `requestAnimationFrame` synchronises animation code with the browser's render loop. Using `transform` instead of `left/top` keeps animation on the compositor thread. `will-change` pre-promotes the element so no layout or paint happens during the animation — but always clean it up afterward to free GPU memory.

sections.title: The 16ms Frame Budget and the Main Thread
sections.content:
At 60 frames per second, the browser has **16.67 milliseconds** between each frame to complete all work: run JavaScript, perform layout, paint changed regions, and composite the frame. Miss this window and a frame is dropped — the screen shows the previous frame again, which users perceive as **jank** (stuttering or choppiness).

The **main thread** is where JavaScript executes, DOM parsing happens, style recalculation runs, and layout is computed. Paint also runs on the main thread (at least the recording of paint commands). Only compositing runs on a separate thread. This means any long-running JavaScript task blocks all of these stages.

**Long tasks** — tasks exceeding 50ms — are considered particularly harmful because they can block user interaction for a noticeable duration. A task that takes 200ms means the page is unresponsive for 200ms: clicks are ignored, keyboard input is not echoed, and if a frame is due during that 200ms window, it is dropped.

**Jank sources in practice**:
1. Expensive recalculate style (complex selectors applied to many elements)
2. Forced synchronous layout inside animation loops
3. Large repaints from animating non-compositor CSS properties
4. Synchronous XHR or heavy JSON parsing on the main thread
5. Excessive DOM nodes (tens of thousands of nodes slow down every pipeline stage)

**The 16ms budget breakdown in practice**: the browser itself needs about 6ms for internal housekeeping (rasterisation, compositing, frame submission). That leaves roughly 10ms for your JavaScript, style recalculation, and layout. This is tighter than it sounds — a single `getComputedStyle()` call on a heavily styled page can take 2-3ms.

Modern browsers expose `PerformanceObserver` with `longtask` entry type to detect tasks exceeding 50ms. The Chrome DevTools Performance tab visualises the pipeline for each frame: green bars are painting, purple bars are layout, yellow are JavaScript. Red triangles mark dropped frames.

The pipelineCost object categorises CSS properties — use this as a mental reference when choosing how to implement animations or dynamic style changes. sections.title: Critical Rendering Path and Performance Optimisation
sections.content:
The **Critical Rendering Path** is the sequence of steps the browser must complete before the first meaningful pixel can be painted: download HTML, parse HTML, download and parse CSS (blocking), potentially execute JavaScript, build Render Tree, layout, paint. Optimising this path reduces **Time to First Contentful Paint (FCP)** — one of Google's Core Web Vitals.

**Key optimisation strategies that follow directly from the pipeline**:

**Minimise render-blocking CSS**: Inline critical CSS (the styles needed for above-the-fold content) directly in the `<head>` in a `<style>` tag. Load non-critical CSS with `media` attributes or dynamically after load. The browser still downloads the non-blocking CSS, but it does not block rendering.

**Use `defer` or `async` for scripts**: `defer` downloads the script in parallel with HTML parsing and executes it after parsing completes (but before `DOMContentLoaded`). `async` downloads in parallel and executes as soon as it is downloaded, potentially interrupting HTML parsing. Both avoid blocking the parser; `defer` is usually preferred for application scripts because it preserves execution order.

**Animate compositor-only properties**: As established, animating `transform` and `opacity` keeps work off the main thread. CSS transitions and animations on these properties are also automatically moved off-thread by the browser when possible.

**Avoid layout thrashing**: Profile first, then apply the batch-reads-before-writes pattern. Libraries like FastDOM provide a queue abstraction that automatically batches reads and writes.

**Use `content-visibility: auto`**: A modern CSS property that skips layout and paint for off-screen elements, significantly reducing rendering cost for long scrolling pages. The browser will calculate the element's size but skip its internal layout until it approaches the viewport.

**Reduce DOM depth and breadth**: Layout performance scales with DOM complexity. A page with 50,000 nodes takes noticeably longer to reflow than one with 5,000. Virtual scrolling and DOM recycling are essential for large lists.

**Avoid universally matched CSS selectors**: Selectors like `* { box-sizing: border-box }` are fine, but complex descendant selectors in frequently-restyled elements add cost to style recalculation. The CSS selector matching order is right-to-left, so `.container .item span em` requires matching every `em` against four ancestors.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions and Edge Cases
sections.content:
**'Virtual DOM eliminates reflow'**: React's Virtual DOM is a technique for batching DOM updates and applying them as a minimal diff. It reduces the number of DOM mutations, which reduces reflow. But the real browser rendering pipeline still runs for every actual DOM change — Virtual DOM does not bypass layout or paint; it minimises what triggers them. For compositor-only animations, Virtual DOM adds no value over direct DOM manipulation with `transform`.

**'opacity:0 is the same as display:none'**: `opacity: 0` makes an element transparent but it remains in the Render Tree, occupies space, participates in layout, receives pointer events (unless `pointer-events: none` is set), and gets painted (then drawn transparently). `display: none` removes it from the Render Tree entirely — no space, no paint, no events. `visibility: hidden` is in between: in the Render Tree, occupies space, but invisible and does not receive pointer events.

**'will-change makes everything faster'**: `will-change` signals intent to the browser, which pre-promotes the element to a compositor layer. This is only beneficial for elements that will actually animate — it uses GPU memory. Over-using it (e.g., `will-change: transform` on hundreds of list items) can exhaust GPU memory and cause more jank than it prevents.

**'CSS animations always run off the main thread'**: Only animations of `transform` and `opacity` on promoted layers can run on the compositor thread. A CSS animation of `width` or `height` still runs on the main thread and triggers layout every frame. The animation syntax (CSS keyframes vs JS) is not what determines the thread — the property being animated determines it.

**'Inline styles are faster than classes'**: Setting `el.style.color = 'red'` and setting `el.classList.add('red')` both trigger style recalculation and potentially paint. Inline styles have higher specificity but similar rendering cost. The real cost is the style recalculation triggered, not the mechanism of applying it.

**'Fixed positioning is free'**: `position: fixed` elements are removed from normal document flow and positioned relative to the viewport. They do get their own compositor layer (which is efficient for scrolling). But they still participate in their stacking context's paint, and if they overlap with content, they can invalidate large repaint regions on every scroll frame.

sections.content: **Historical context**: Early browsers (Netscape, IE4) had no concept of incremental layout or compositing — every DOM change triggered a full page repaint. The notion of a separate compositor thread was pioneered by Apple's WebKit team around 2007-2010 for Safari on iOS, where GPU compositing was essential for achieving smooth scrolling on limited hardware. Chrome adopted and extended this model, and the compositing architecture we use today was largely standardised by 2012. The key insight — that `transform` and `opacity` can be animated without touching layout or paint — is a direct consequence of GPU texture compositing and remains the cornerstone of smooth web animation.

**Interview and performance audit insights**: When asked 'why is this animation janky?', the answer is almost always one of: (1) animating a layout-triggering property instead of `transform`; (2) layout thrashing — alternating reads and writes; (3) a long JavaScript task blocking the main thread; or (4) excessive paint area from a large `box-shadow` or gradient on a frequently-changed element. The three-question diagnostic: **which CSS property is being animated? Is there a read-write interleave in the animation loop? How long does the heaviest JS task take?** In DevTools, the Performance panel answers all three: look for purple Layout bars inside frames, yellow JS bars, and long tasks highlighted in red. The flame chart drill-down will point to the exact function causing the bottleneck.

items: **The rendering pipeline** has six stages: DOM construction → CSSOM construction → Render Tree assembly → Layout (reflow) → Paint (rasterisation) → Composite. Each stage feeds the next, and JavaScript changes to DOM or CSS can re-trigger stages from anywhere in the pipeline.

**CSSOM is render-blocking**: the browser will not paint a single pixel until all CSS is downloaded and parsed. Large or slow-loading stylesheets directly delay First Contentful Paint — inline critical CSS and use `media` attributes to make non-critical CSS non-blocking.

**Layout (reflow) is the most expensive stage**: it computes geometry for every affected node recursively. Anything that changes element size or position triggers it. Minimize reflows by batching DOM writes together and reading layout properties only once, before any writes.

**Layout thrashing** — alternating DOM reads (`offsetWidth`, `getBoundingClientRect`) and writes in a loop — forces N synchronous layout calculations instead of one deferred layout. Always batch all reads before all writes, or use `requestAnimationFrame` to align with the render loop.

**`transform` and `opacity` are compositor-only**: animating these properties on a promoted layer bypasses layout and paint entirely, running on the GPU thread at ~60fps even when the main thread is busy. They are the only safe properties for smooth, jank-free animation.

**`will-change` pre-promotes an element** to a GPU compositor layer, eliminating layout and paint during animation — but each promoted layer consumes GPU texture memory. Use it sparingly on elements that will actually animate, and remove it afterward with `will-change: auto`.

**The 16.67ms frame budget** (1000ms ÷ 60fps) is shared among JavaScript, style recalculation, layout, paint, and composite. Long tasks (>50ms) block all rendering and make the page feel unresponsive. Use `PerformanceObserver` with `type:'longtask'` and Chrome DevTools Performance tab to diagnose frame budget violations.

quiz.question: Which CSS property change triggers ONLY the Composite stage, making it the cheapest animation choice?
options: background-color
width
opacity
margin-top
quiz.explanation: `opacity` (along with `transform`) can be animated purely on the GPU compositor thread — no layout or paint is needed. `background-color` triggers paint but not layout. `width` and `margin-top` both trigger layout, paint, and composite — the most expensive path.

quiz.question: What is 'layout thrashing' and why does it happen?
options: Using too many CSS animations simultaneously, overwhelming the GPU
Alternating DOM writes with layout property reads in a loop, causing repeated forced synchronous layouts
Applying complex CSS selectors that require many matching passes
Rendering too many compositor layers, exhausting GPU memory
quiz.explanation: Layout thrashing occurs when JavaScript alternates writes (mutating the DOM) with reads of layout properties like `offsetWidth` or `getBoundingClientRect`. Each read after a write forces the browser to synchronously complete pending layout before returning a value. Repeating this N times in a loop causes N layout calculations instead of one. The fix is to batch all reads before any writes.

quiz.question: Why is CSSOM construction render-blocking but DOM construction is not?
options: CSS files are always larger and slower to parse than HTML
The browser cannot render anything until all styles are known, because a later stylesheet could override earlier styles and cause visual inconsistency
JavaScript always executes before CSS can be applied
CSSOM requires a separate CPU core to construct
quiz.explanation: The browser blocks rendering until the entire CSSOM is built because any CSS file loaded later could completely change the appearance of already-parsed elements. Rendering partial CSS would cause a flash of unstyled content. HTML parsing, by contrast, can proceed incrementally — partial DOM is valid. This is why large unneeded CSS files hurt Time to First Paint.

quiz.question: Which DOM read operation forces a synchronous layout flush when called after a DOM write?
options: element.textContent
element.getAttribute('data-id')
element.getBoundingClientRect()
element.dataset.value
quiz.explanation: `getBoundingClientRect()` requires up-to-date layout geometry. If there are pending DOM mutations, the browser must synchronously complete layout before returning the result. `textContent`, `getAttribute`, and `dataset` do not require layout information and can be read without triggering a layout flush.

quiz.question: How does `will-change: transform` improve animation performance, and what is its cost?
options: It pre-computes the animation keyframes and caches them, saving CPU time during playback
It promotes the element to its own GPU compositor layer, so transform changes bypass layout and paint — at the cost of GPU texture memory
It moves the element's JavaScript event handlers to a worker thread
It disables style inheritance for the element, speeding up CSSOM traversal
quiz.explanation: `will-change: transform` hints to the browser to pre-promote the element to a GPU compositor layer. Transform changes to that layer then require only a compositing step — no layout or paint — enabling smooth animation. The cost is GPU texture memory: one layer per promoted element, roughly 4 bytes × pixel area. Over-using it exhausts GPU memory and causes worse performance.

quiz.question: An element has `display: none`. Where does it appear in the browser's internal trees?
options: Both DOM and Render Tree
DOM only — it is excluded from the Render Tree
Render Tree only — the DOM skips invisible elements
Neither the DOM nor the Render Tree
quiz.explanation: `display: none` elements ARE in the DOM — they exist as objects, can be selected with `querySelector`, and have attributes and children. But they are excluded from the Render Tree because they occupy no space and are not painted. `visibility: hidden` elements ARE in the Render Tree — they take up space but render as transparent.

quiz.question: Animating CSS `left` vs `transform: translateX()` — what is the key performance difference?
options: `left` runs on the GPU; `transform` is CPU-only and therefore slower
`transform: translateX()` only works on block-level elements
Animating `left` triggers layout recalculation every frame; `transform: translateX()` only triggers compositing on the GPU thread
They are equivalent because CSS animations always run on a dedicated animation thread
quiz.explanation: Animating `left` changes an element's position in the document flow, triggering Layout → Paint → Composite on every frame at 60fps. Animating `transform: translateX()` operates only at the Composite stage — it applies a GPU matrix transform to an already-painted texture. This is why transform-based movement is smooth while `left/top` animations cause jank.

quiz.question: What is the browser's per-frame time budget for rendering at 60 frames per second?
options: ~8ms
~33ms
quiz.explanation: 1000ms ÷ 60fps = 16.67ms per frame. Within this budget the browser must complete JavaScript execution, style recalculation, layout, paint, and compositing. The browser itself needs ~6ms for internal work, leaving roughly 10ms for application JS and layout. Tasks exceeding 50ms are classified as 'long tasks' and make pages feel unresponsive.

quiz.question: A CSS pseudo-element (`::before`) is visible on screen. Where does it appear in the browser's trees?
options: In the DOM and the Render Tree
In the DOM only
In the Render Tree but not the DOM
In neither tree — it is handled directly by the paint stage
quiz.explanation: Pseudo-elements like `::before` and `::after` are generated by CSS rules and inserted into the Render Tree as if they were child nodes. However, they have no corresponding DOM nodes — `document.querySelector('::before')` returns null. They affect layout and are painted normally, but exist only in the rendering model, not in the JavaScript-accessible DOM.

quiz.question: Which API correctly responds to element size changes without polling or triggering forced layout recalculations?
options: MutationObserver with `subtree: true`
IntersectionObserver with `threshold: 0`
ResizeObserver
PerformanceObserver with `type: 'layout-shift'`
quiz.explanation: `ResizeObserver` fires a callback whenever an observed element's content box dimensions change, delivering size information without requiring polling loops. Its callback is called after layout, so reading sizes inside it is safe. `MutationObserver` watches DOM structure and attribute changes. `IntersectionObserver` detects viewport visibility. `PerformanceObserver` with `layout-shift` tracks Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) metrics, not individual element sizes.
